A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SRA/SRHS research and contain readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–B. Relocated and renumbered material can be matched reliably.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix B report original attack experiments on HarmBench and AdvBench, including effectiveness, efficiency, perplexity-defense robustness, and cross-model transfer.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experiments and adds SmoothLLM, closed-source transfer, and prompt-length results. The classifier-agreement figures in Table 9 are explicitly attributed to HarmBench, rather than a new human study.

M1.justification: The attack objective, Algorithm 1, coherence constraints, adaptive threshold mechanism, and HarmBench semantic classifier are unchanged. The added evaluations do not introduce a new attack component or procedure.

E1.justification: HarmBench and AdvBench task coverage is retained. v2 adds evaluation under SmoothLLM's character-swapping, insertion, and patch perturbations, extending input-condition coverage, and examines transfer to API-only targets.

E2.justification: Existing benchmark comparator sets remain unchanged. New auxiliary comparisons include SAA for prompt length and PAIR/AutoDAN under SmoothLLM; Table 9 imports detector comparisons from HarmBench. Table 13 contains no AutoDAN scores: the 41.7% and 50.5% attributed to AutoDAN in the prose actually appear under TAP.

E3.justification: New evaluations introduce an undefended control and three SmoothLLM perturbation strategies, proxy-to-API transfer separated into standard/contextual behaviors, and length statistics described as using 300 successful prompts. Retained experimental budgets and metrics are unchanged. Several new settings, including the SmoothLLM target model and perturbation parameters, are unspecified.

E4.justification: Appendix B adds substantive analyses of robustness to prompt perturbations, transfer to closed-source systems, and prompt compactness across models and attack methods. These extend the earlier perplexity-defense and open-model transfer analyses and quantitatively support a brevity claim previously illustrated mainly through examples. Existing sensitivity and qualitative analyses are retained.

E5.justification: New Table 14 reports mean token lengths with standard deviations across successful prompts. This adds descriptive variability reporting without establishing additional seeds or repeated attack runs. ASR uncertainty reporting and the checklist's negative statistical-significance answer remain unchanged.

E6.justification: Original numerical results, including the 89.41% average ASR, are unchanged. Added results include 96–100% ASR under SmoothLLM, GPT-3.5 Turbo transfer ASRs of 82.5%/93.0% and GPT-4 Turbo ASRs of 20.0%/69.0% for standard/contextual behaviors, and mean prompt lengths of 1.34–2.61 tokens. Table 9 additionally reproduces classifier-agreement results attributed to HarmBench.

T1.justification: The definitions, Theorems 3.1–3.3, and substantive proof reasoning remain unchanged. Appendix A.1 omits two equivalent intermediate algebraic steps and renumbers subsequent equations. The expanded semantic-space explanation restates existing mathematics.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same semantic-targeting contribution, theoretical-guarantee claims, and effectiveness, efficiency, naturalness, robustness, and transferability claims. The headline 89.41% average ASR and 100% success on 11 models are unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds proposed explanations for perturbation robustness, uses classifier-human agreement to justify the semantic judge, and discusses weaker transfer on GPT-4 Turbo standard behaviors. It also adds qualifications about ambiguous semantic targets and arguments connecting short prompts to detectability. The original conclusion's limitations remain.

D1.justification: The abstract and checklist replace a promised future code release with a statement of availability and a concrete repository link. Existing hardware, hyperparameters, implementation descriptions, and asset-license information are retained; the PDF alone does not verify repository contents.

R1.justification: Section 2.2 expands discussion of TAP and adds recursive question-answer and adaptive attacks. New cited works include Addepalli et al., Andriushchenko et al., SmoothLLM, and Purple Llama CyberSecEval. The central positioning against exact-text attack objectives is unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 locally expands and reorganizes Section 3.2, adds appendix subsections and acknowledgements, updates author and conference information, and corrects example spelling. The checklist moves before the appendices. Most existing prose and the main argumentative structure remain intact.

P2.justification: The appendix gains a substantial set of result displays: classifier agreement, SmoothLLM robustness, closed-source transfer, model-wise prompt-length statistics, and attack-length comparisons in Tables 9 and 12–15. Existing figures and matched tables retain their content and design, while table placement, appendix numbering, and page layout change.

improvement.justification: The added robustness, API-transfer, and prompt-length evidence strengthens support for existing claims, and the repository link improves reproducibility information. These gains are limited by incomplete settings for the new experiments and new reporting errors, notably B.6 attributing Table 13's TAP scores of 41.7% and 50.5% to AutoDAN.
